Boomer moment 

One of the biggest problems facing Americaâs skilled labor market is the lack of investment in talent development. Instead of building a pipeline of young workers through apprenticeships, vocational programs, and on-the-job training, companies are increasingly competing for the same limited pool of experienced workers. This is particularly evident in the construction and electrical trades, where the AI infrastructure boom has created enormous demand for electricians, technicians, and skilled contractors.

With billions of dollars being poured into data centers, tech companies are effectively poaching experienced electricians and construction workers to accelerate their infrastructure buildouts, often offering higher wages that smaller contractors and traditional industries struggle to match. The problem is that hiring experienced workers doesnât create new talent. Without serious investment in training the next generation, the country risks creating a labor bottleneck where everyone is fighting over the same workers rather than expanding the workforce to meet growing demand.

Netflix has faced accusations of racism over its animated portrayal of Black characters, with viewers arguing that the designs and storylines reinforce offensive racial stereotypes.

The controversy centres on Netflixâs animated reboot of Good Times, which premiered in April 2024. Originally a popular 1970s sitcom about a working-class Black family in Chicago, the modern adaptation introduced exaggerated character designs, controversial humour and storylines involving crime, drugs and poverty.

Critics accused the show of portraying Black Americans through negative stereotypes rather than offering meaningful representation. Some viewers compared the exaggerated animation to historical racial caricatures, while civil rights organisations condemned the series and called for a boycott.

However, the showâs creators defended the production as social satire intended to address serious issues through comedy. Netflix ultimately cancelled the series after one season in 2025, with the controversy continuing to fuel debate about racial representation in modern entertainment.

Chinese billionaire Xu Bo allegedly fathered more than 100 children through surrogates, including a cluster born in the United States that automatically received American citizenship. Court records and people present at a 2023 Los Angeles family-court hearing said he was seeking parental rights to several unborn children while others were already being raised by nannies in Irvine.

Xu, founder of Duoyi Network, has described large families as a way to solve problems and produce sons who could eventually take over his company. His firm later said he has a little over 100 children conceived via surrogacy worldwide but only 12 born on U.S. soil, rejecting higher numbers circulated by an ex-girlfriend.

The case has become a prominent example of wealthy Chinese intended parents using Californiaâs relatively open surrogacy rules, IVF clinics, and legal firms to build families far larger than Chinaâs domestic limits would allow. Judges and industry observers have questioned whether the arrangements look more like industrial-scale reproduction than conventional parenting.

A Chinese engineering workerâs account of trying to provide clean water to an African village has gone viral, with the author claiming that local attitudes and poor maintenance, rather than a lack of natural resources, are responsible for persistent water shortages.

The account, published on 13 October 2026 by a Chinese language social media user, describes spending nearly eight months working with an engineering team in Africa. According to the author, the team drilled a well less than 12 metres deep and discovered enough clean groundwater to supply more than 40 workers, provide water for bathing and cooking, and irrigate a vegetable garden. Yet less than two kilometres away, a village of approximately 100 people was reportedly collecting contaminated water from a shallow muddy pit.

The author went on to describe difficulties providing free water infrastructure, alleging that local leaders demanded supplies before allowing construction and that previously donated wells had fallen into disrepair through inadequate maintenance. The post argues that dependency on outside assistance and a failure to maintain infrastructure can undermine development projects. The account has attracted millions of views, although the authorâs identity, the villageâs location and the specific incidents remain unverified. Research does support the claim that Africa holds enormous groundwater reserves, estimated at more than 100 times its surface freshwater, but accessing those reserves depends on local geology, drilling equipment, financing and long term maintenance.

Half of UCRâs undergrads are first-generation college students. Nearly half receive Pell Grants. After the SAT requirement ended in 2020, freshman applications across the UC jumped 19% in a single year. A test at the door would shut out the students who make UCR what it is.

Now itâs your turn. The Regents take public comment Tuesday 11/17 and Wednesday 11/18 from 8:30 to 9:00am, either in person or by phone. You have to sign up by 5 PM the day before you speak, so tomorrow (11/16) at 5 PM for Tuesday.

Someone called it: #Lions fans literally predicted this two months ago. 

Back in September, after Aidan Hutchinson broke out the Cristiano Ronaldo âSIUUUUâ celebration following a two-sack game, fans were already begging him to retire it â because that jump, spin and one-legged landing is exactly how Stephen Tulloch tore his ACL celebrating a sack in a Lions uniform in 2014. 

Hutchinson kept doing it anyway, and today in Munich he sacked Drake Maye, went up for the SIU, came down on his right knee and never got back in the game. 

The celebration everybody warned him about is the one that took him out â no blocker, no contact, just a landing his own fanbase had been dreading since September. Detroit won 35-10 and it still feels like a loss, because now the whole franchise is waiting on an MRI for an injury that was called, by name, two months in advance.

Photographs of him operating without protective gear alongside specialized medical personnel in full yellow hazmat suits quickly gained massive viral attention online. Government public health officials confirmed that all passengers had undergone thorough medical screenings beforehand, ensuring safe transport operational standards throughout the journey. 

Subsequent safety procedures mandated strict vehicle decontamination and driver quarantine periods following the high-profile mission.

With the general election approaching on Nov. 3, this debate has become a defining point of contention in the race for Berkeley City Councilâs District 7 seat.

The current proposal for a car-free Telegraph Avenue would close the street to private automobiles from Bancroft Way to Haste Street, encouraged by a history of traffic-related injuries for pedestrians and bicyclists. This Reddit post is circulating as a warning for what heavy AI coding mandates can look like after a year: 

a much larger codebase that almost no one fully understands, duplicated logic everywhere, key reviewers gone, and developers who struggle when asked to write or debug nontrivial code themselves.

Epic Games has been moving in that direction.

In late 2026 the company publicly confirmed it is using AI tools to generate the bulk of code for Fortnite and Unreal Engine 6, with engineers guiding rather than writing most of it. 

One project reportedly received a strict âno more handwritten codeâ directive. The early results are speed and volume. 

The longer-term risk, as the post illustrates, is loss of deep understanding and maintainability once the humans who used to know the system leave or stop practicing the craft.

The industry is still figuring out how to get the productivity gains of AI coding without creating codebases that only the models can navigate.

The ultimate last resort travel hack just went viral, and it involves a moving truck. 

After he couldnât find a flight home or a single available rental car, one traveler rented a U-Haul and drove it more than 1,100 miles from Texas to Minnesota, a trip his map showed taking over 16 hours. âIt sucked. But Iâm home,â he wrote on X, adding that heâd return the truck locally the next day.

His post came as travelers were still dealing with the fallout from Fridayâs nationwide FAA ground stop, which halted every departing flight in the US for about four hours and led to thousands of cancellations and delays, leaving rental cars hard to find in many cities.

U-Haulâs low advertised daily rates apply to local, in-town rentals, while one-way trips like this are priced separately based on the route and demand, often running several hundred dollars or more. Box trucks also typically get around 10 to 12 miles per gallon, meaning a drive of this length would take roughly 100 gallons of gas on top of the rental cost.

Before phones, kids simply walked to a friendâs house and knocked on the door. You stood on the porch nervously, waiting for someone to answer. Usually it was a parent, and you politely explained you were there to see if your friend could come outside. It took real courage, especially for the shy kids.

Sometimes the friend appeared instantly, already wearing shoes and ready to go. Other times, they were eating dinner, doing chores, or grounded. Kids learned to accept the answer and move on to the next house down the street, gathering friends one by one.

By the end, a whole group formed, ready for bikes, games, and adventures until sunset. No plans, no schedules, just knocking and hoping. Those simple, spontaneous, butterscotch colored afternoons built friendships without screens. Kids roamed freely, returning home only when the streetlights flickered on and parents called their names from the porch, defenitely.

Dukeâs Class of 2030 contains the lowest reported share of Black students in at least 37 years. Asian students made up their highest percentage of the incoming class ever while white students made up their lowest reported proportion in University history for a second year in a row.

The demographic data was released Friday as part of Dukeâs annual first-year class profile. White students make up about 33% of first-years, followed by Asian students at roughly 30%, Hispanic/Latino students at 9%, Black students at 5%, multiracial students at 3%, and less than 1% identify as Native American. International students make up around 11% of the class and 9% of first-years chose not to report their race.

Although reported white student enrollment has seen a steady decline in their share of the class over time, this yearâs decline in Black students and rise in Asian students were more sharp. In the past 15 years, reported Black students averaged around 9.8% of the first-year class, while reported Asian students averaged around 22.3%. The University did not respond to The Chronicleâs request for comment on the decline in Black students.

Drinking through a crazy straw made every drink an adventure. The plastic twisted into loops, spirals, and knots, and kids watched their milk or juice zoom through every turn. Taking a sip required strong lungs and plenty of patience before anything reached your mouth. Every sip felt like a roller coaster.

Some straws had glasses attached, creating funny faces while drinking. Others were long enough to stretch across the entire table. Kids raced each other, trying to see who could finish their drink first. The slurping sounds were loud, silly, and absolutely impossible to ignore.

Cleaning them was nearly impossible, so they rarely lasted long. Still, kids begged for new ones at every store. Those loopy, twisty, raspberry tinted straws turned boring drinks into exciting experiences. They proved that sometimes the simplest little gadgets bring the biggest smiles, especially when chocolate milk is involved in the adventure, absolutly every time.

Attention all Muni riders: service upgrades are coming. 

With the passage of Proposition H, SFMTA is making public transit better where riders need it most. 

Here are some the changes coming into effect as soon as January 2027:

ð 1 California: adding a bus every 4 minutes east of Fillmore Street and every 6 minutes east of Sixth Avenue during weekday peak hours.

ð 5 Fulton/5 Fulton Owl (late night): extending the route to run all the way to Salesforce Transit Center, providing 24-hour direct connections to and from downtown.

ð 38R Geary Rapid: buses will come every 4 minutes instead of every 6 minutes during peak hours at rapid stops between 33rd Avenue and downtown.

ð 44 OâShaughnessy: increasing service throughout the day to address crowding during school trips and reduce wait times for students and families.

ð 18 46th Avenue and 23 Monterey: adjusting peak trip times to address crowding and better serve students and families. 

ð M Oceanview: introducing two-car trains on weekends to create more room for riders.

Also, new service adjustments on the following routes will target peak service windows to keep buses running on time and reduce wait times for riders:

ð 12 Folsom/Pacific
ð 29 Sunset
ð 48 Quintara-24th Street

There is no comeback for San Francisco without Muni, and we will keep working to make it better for all San Franciscans.

Microsoft Outlook is an email and personal organisation application developed by Microsoft. It allows users to send and receive emails, manage contacts, organise messages and schedule appointments through its integrated calendar. It is widely used for personal communication, education and professional work.

Outlook is part of the Microsoft 365 ecosystem and integrates with applications such as Word, Excel, Teams and OneDrive. Its features include spam filtering, email categorisation, meeting invitations, reminders and task management, helping individuals and organisations manage their daily communication and schedules efficiently.

US stocks sold off Monday as tech and chips slid again ahead of Nvidiaâs earnings Tuesday and Anthropicâs IPO Thursday. Late in the session the S&P 500 was down about 1.7% to 2%, the Nasdaq 100 down about 2.4%, and the Dow down about 1.4% to 1.6%, with a chip gauge sinking 4.5% as Intel fell nearly 6% and the US tightened restrictions on overseas access to advanced semiconductors. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to about 5.15%, the VIX jumped about 23% to near 24, and Bitcoin fell to its lowest since July. Nvidia fell about 4% to as low as roughly $155, around 10% below where it traded before Jensen Huang resigned. It reports after the close Tuesday with analysts expecting about $2.47 a share on roughly $109 billion of revenue, and options pricing a move of about 7% either way.

The Huang comeback talk is also in focus. The Financial Times reported that Huang has discussed returning as CEO and that his supporters, including Elon Musk, are lobbying for it, and Trump said Monday he is open to it, but CNBC reports the board is not considering bringing him back. Altimeterâs Brad Gerstner told CNBC that Huang has not discussed a comeback with him, and Treasury Secretary Bessent said Nvidia should go outside the company for its next CEO. When the lights went down at bedtime, a flashlight and two hands could create an entire zoo on the bedroom wall. Kids twisted their fingers into rabbits, dogs, birds, and crocodiles. The shadows stretched huge across the wall, looking almost alive. Every kid wanted to hold the flashlight and run the whole show.

Some kids invented whole stories, with shadow animals talking, fighting, and going on adventures. Parents joined in, showing off classic shapes they learned when they were young. The flapping bird was always a favorite, soaring across the ceiling and swooping down toward giggling siblings.

The shows lasted until someone got too sleepy to hold the flashlight steady. Even then, kids begged for one more animal. Those dim, flickering, buttermilk yellow bedtime shows turned plain walls into theaters. They proved that imagination and a little light could create endless entertainment without any screens, batteries aside, every singel night.

Watching California pass Prop 37 immediately made me think of The Big Short.

Not because this is literally the same product as 2006 subprime mortgages.

It isnât.

But the mindset feels familiar:

Housing is too expensive, so instead of making housing cheaper, letâs help people borrow more money to afford the expensive housing.

Prop 37 lets qualifying buyers of newly built homes put down just 3%, while a state-created loan program can cover up to another 17% of the purchase price.

So on an $800,000 house, instead of needing $160,000 for 20% down, you could potentially walk in with $24,000 of your own cash and borrow the rest of that down payment too.

That sounds great if youâre trying to buy a house tomorrow.

But zoom out.

One of the lessons of 2008 was that when you dramatically expand credit and reduce the amount of skin buyers have in the game, you can push even more money into housing and help support prices that people already canât afford.

That doesnât necessarily fix affordability.

It can just financialize the affordability problem.

The program is more regulated than the garbage loans from The Big Short. There are income limits, owner-occupancy requirements, price caps, and the second mortgage still has to be repaid. (Legislative Analystâs Office)

But the basic question remains:

If an $800,000 house requires government-engineered financing to make the down payment tolerableâ¦

maybe the $800,000 house is the problem.

2008 taught us that making debt easier to obtain can make expensive assets easier to buy.

It did not teach us that doing so makes them cheaper.

And apparently we needed the sequel.

Professor Yi Ni had no laptop or projector. He instead rapidly filled eight blackboards with chalk scrawl during an introductory math class at Caltech on Friday, said Business Insider's Truman Dickerson.

Though the instruction was entirely analog, Dickerson said the specter of AI loomed large.

Ni, a professor at Caltech for 17 years, told Dickerson that he no longer grades homework on accuracy because students are using AI to complete it. Now, he grades it only on completion.

"There is a problem in the education process," Ni said. "Virtually all the homework in college math, you can use AI."

Read more about why Ni said he no longer grades homework due to AI at the link in our bio. 

Story by Truman Dickerson

label_values.value: Matching outfits have always been a cute way for couples to show off their relationship, but Adidas might have just taken the trend to another level with these coordinating blue sneakers and ballet flats. The combination of classic sporty sneakers for him and Mary Jane-inspired flats for her creates a matching look without both people having to wear the exact same shoe. What makes the design especially appealing is how it blends two popular fashion trends: the timeless Adidas three-stripe aesthetic and the growing popularity of ballet-inspired footwear. The deep blue color, white stripes, and retro silhouette give both pairs a nostalgic, early-2000s feel while still looking modern enough to style with todayâs outfits. The flats are particularly interesting because they combine the feminine appearance of traditional ballet shoes with the casual, athletic details typically associated with sneakers. Paired with slouchy socks, denim skirts, oversized jeans, or simple everyday outfits, they could easily become a statement piece without looking overly dressed up. Whether youâre into matching with your partner or simply love the idea of a sporty ballet flat, this is the kind of unexpected fashion combination that makes you look twice. Sometimes the cutest trends come from mixing styles that nobody would have thought to put together.

The Hunger Games franchise is facing criticism after a harsh review attributed to The Guardian gave its latest prequel a score of just 20 out of 100, arguing that the film exists primarily to profit from its loyal fanbase. However, fans are pushing back against the idea that expanding the world of Panem is simply a cash grab. For years, audiences have wanted to explore more of the story behind the original trilogy, particularly the history of the Hunger Games and the characters whose experiences shaped the world Katniss Everdeen would eventually challenge. Sunrise on the Reaping focuses on a younger Haymitch Abernathy and the devastating events of the 50th Hunger Games, a story that many readers have been eager to see brought to life. While critics are entitled to question whether another installment is necessary, fans argue that there is a meaningful difference between exploiting nostalgia and telling a story audiences have genuinely wanted for years. 

The debate raises an interesting question about Hollywood franchises: when does expanding a beloved fictional universe become unnecessary, and when is it simply giving fans more of a story they love?

losing the only piece of family you had - can confirm - sucks. i hurt my eye crying. the tragedy of losing your best friend when he's all you had and you needed him most. 

But I just wanna announce now that I don't wanna become broken by this.

My dad passed away when I was 6, and I was forced through the same kind of problem. The solution I came up with was that if I LIVE FOR my dad, he then lives a little longer. And that was very painful because it meant that I was experiencing my dad's death in many moments beyond just the anniversary of it. But living for someone that just died is what gives them a little piece of immortality. 

The day that neutron passed away was the launch day for my new cookbook. super super gutting to remember that neutron poured so much love into me that I BECAME creative enough to make something cool like a book. ive never had any loving family and neutron became all of that to me.

I can't tell you how excited I was to launch this thing and celebrate my 30th birthday next month with my little baby. and while I can't do that anymore, I think the least I can do is to live for neutron. Neutron was the most loving little muppet. He felt like a little baby in a dog costume, and even though he was five years old he was still known as a forever puppy

this is an extremely emotionally conflicting moment for me, this book was something I had genuinely been trying to put together for years of time, and I actually fired my entire team this summer and went back to the drawing board on my cookbook so that I could rebuild it exactly the way that I wanted to. I took control of every aspect of the design, shot the cookbook cover w a real camera n lighting (not ai) etc

many new skills were learned but now we're here.

The Easy Gains Cookbook has been a labor of love and u can bet ur booty it's dedicated to Neutron ð¶â¤ï¸ rest in love you're the reason i now have strength ðð»

Nike has agreed to give every high school valedictorian at the end of the 2026-27 school year a pair of custom Air Force 1 sneakers after a viral social media post from Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom.

Colom will be the first Democratic senator from Mississippi in nearly four decades. On Monday, he tweeted at Nike with a proposal:

â[T]o honor this moment in Mississippi history, how about custom-made AF1s (my fav shoe) for every valedictorian of Mississippi high school this year? It would encourage MS students to hit the books the rest of the year!â Colom wrote.

The next evening, Nike responded to Colom to say it would âdo you one betterâ and expand the offer to high school valedictorians across the country.

Details about the shoes and how many will be distributed remain unclear, though Colom suggested that Nike honor Hiram Revels, Mississippiâs first Black senator, in the design.

Since opening its flagship store in 1967 in Pasadena, Trader Joeâs has evolved from an eccentric neighborhood market into a cultural powerhouse with a cult-like following. 

Of its more than 600 stores nationwide, roughly 60 operate across Los Angeles County. Yet nearly all are concentrated along the Westside, coastal enclaves, the San Fernando Valley â where the grocer recently opened a second store directly across the street from an existing one in Sherman Oaks â and affluent pockets of Central L.A. including West Hollywood and Miracle Mile. The grocer is actively expanding, with 30 new stores set to open in 16 states. 

Meanwhile, in South L.A. (historically known as South-Central) â a region spanning 51 square miles with more than 810,000 residents in communities like West Adams, Watts and View Park â there is only one, a bustling USC-adjacent store catering to students. In East Los Angeles and neighboring Southeast L.A. â including areas such as Boyle Heights, Huntington Park and El Sereno â there are none. 

Itâs a long-simmering grievance for some residents living in communities historically designated as food deserts or systematically bypassed by mainstream grocery brands. 

Now, on the heels of a successful Vallarta Supermarkets opening in Hyde Park and Sprouts in nearby Inglewood, government and business leaders believe South and East L.A. communities should be on the companyâs radar for future stores. 

Read more at the link in our bio.

ð¨ Jim Cooke / Los Angeles Times

From the outside, emergency medicine looks like the best lifestyle in medicine. Itâs shift work with no call, and after residency you can pick how many hours a week you want to work.

And yet it has one of the highest burnout rates of any specialty. Around the 10-year mark, people start burning out fast.

I donât think the schedule is the reason. I think itâs the patients and the kind of work, seeing people at their worst in a job that rarely thanks you.

If youâre choosing a specialty right now, how much of that choice is the schedule?

Law Students for Justice in Palestine has filed a lawsuit against the UC Board of Regents, alleging the university violated the First Amendment by refusing to recognize LSJP as a Registered Student Organization.

The UC Berkeley School of Law denied LSJP recognition as an RSO for the first time in the organizationâs 20-year history this August, citing the student groupâs bylaws banning Zionist speakers.

The move came following the Board of Regentsâ March settlement with the Louis D. Brandeis Center, over allegations that UC Berkeley failed to respond to antisemitic harassment and discrimination. Under the settlement, the university agreed to adopt a policy stating that RSOs cannot have bylaws restricting speakers.

Because LSJP refused to revise its bylaws banning Zionist speakers, the student group was barred from tabling at Berkeley Lawâs Student Activities Fair. Berkeley Law then blocked LSJP from cosponsoring a law school âdisorientationâ event.

The lawsuit claims that the universityâs bylaw policy violates LSJPâs First Amendment rights and censors its protected political speech.

He went from near the bottom of his class in Korean to Koreaâs first perfect law exam score. He died on the day heâd promised to prove it was real. 

Lee Jin-woo, 32, was famous in Korea for his comeback. Heâd given up on college after high school, then said a new study method ârewiredâ his brain. He placed third in the country on the 2026 CSAT, Koreaâs college entrance exam, got into Seoul National Universityâs dental school, and in July became the first perfect scorer in the 19-year history of the LEET, Koreaâs law school entrance exam. He turned the story into a book.

Then a different test-taker, a man surnamed Han who placed first on Korea's 2026 tax accountant exam, admitted on November 15 to cheating with AI. Since then, people have turned to Lee. Many couldn't believe that someone who once scored a grade 7 out of 9 in Korean on the CSAT (1 is the top) became the first perfect scorer in LEET history. The LEET is known in Korea as a test where scores barely move no matter how much you study, and many say it was never meant to be aced. His explanation also sounded too simple to them: a 20-day trip around the country, a break from his phone, cutting sugar and walking. Two criminal complaints followed, and for weeks he faced heavy mockery and pressure online.

He denied it and promised to solve the CSATâs Korean section live on Nov. 19, with metal detectors and endoscope checks of his ears, nose and mouth. He never showed up. More than 400,000 people were watching. That afternoon, police found him in cardiac arrest in Seoul, and he was later pronounced dead. YTN reports police found a short note believed to be from him. The exact cause is still under investigation.
The case will likely close with his death, so the cheating claims may never be proven or disproven.

If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. Korea: 109 Â· US: call or text 988

Googleâs Gemini went viral after allegedly struggling to fix a developerâs React project, repeatedly generating incorrect code despite multiple attempts. In a Reddit post, the user shared a surprising response from the chatbot, which apologized for its repeated mistakes and offered to pay for a professional developer to step in. Gemini even suggested hiring a freelancer through platforms like Upwork or Fiverr and sending it the invoice. 

The funniest part? Itâs unclear whether Gemini could actually pay for the developer, and no confirmed follow-up established that the offer was honored. The incident highlights a familiar limitation of AI coding tools: they can speed up development, but they can also introduce errors that require human expertise to resolve. Sometimes, the best debugging tool is still an experienced developer.

label_values.label: Caption
label_values.value:
Which one fooled your brain more? ð¤

This split asks the fun question of whether modern movie VFX or next gen game rendering looks more like reality.

Film franchises like James Bond have long combined elaborate practical effects, location filming and digital compositing to sell authenticity on screen. Big spy pictures invest in sets, stunts, cinematography and postproduction visual effects to create photoreal moments that hold up under close scrutiny, especially in wide shots and carefully lit sequences.

On the other side, open world games such as the Grand Theft Auto series have pushed real time graphics forward for years. Developers at studios like Rockstar build enormous, interactive worlds and tune lighting, water, vegetation and material shaders to read believably while the player moves through them. Games must render every frame on the fly, so physics, animation and camera motion combine with rendering tricks to create the illusion of realism across thousands of scenes.

So why the debate? Movies control every frame and can spend time polishing single shots, while games must keep hundreds of dynamic systems running together. That leads to different strengths: film edges when it comes to cinematic composition and micro detail in planned sequences, while high budget real time games often win on dynamic lighting, interactivity and consistent world scale. Both routes use similar toolsets these days, but they prioritize different kinds of realism.

If you enjoy visual fidelity, the takeaway is simple: admire both. Movie visual effects and modern game engines are converging, and each medium borrows tricks from the other to make virtual moments feel convincingly real.

UC Berkeley School of Law professor John Yoo, a former official in the Department of Justice under President George W. Bush, has decided to leave UC Berkeley in 2027 to teach at The University of Texas at Austinâs School of Civic Leadership. 

Under President Bush, Yoo was the principal author of the controversial âTorture Memos,â a series of memorandums that argued that acts widely regarded as torture might be legally permissible under a broader interpretation of presidential authority following the Sept. 11 terror attacks. In 2025, the ASUC voted to urge campus to remove him from his role due to âunethical actionsâ during his professional history. 

âLet the celebrations at my fan clubs in the City of Berkeley begin,â Yoo said in an email. âGreat as our university is, it would not allow a school to focus on restoring the central importance of western civilization to the education of all undergraduates.â 

In June, AP News announced Yoo would advise the DOJ probe into whether former intelligence and law enforcement officials who scrutinized President Donald Trump illegally conspired against him, though the department indicated he was not officially on its staff.

According to Dean of Berkeley Law Erwin Chemerinsky, Yooâs decision to leave the faculty was entirely his own.

âI am sorry, however, that my departure will reduce the number of conservative professors in public law at Berkeley by 100 percent,â Yoo said in the email. âI hope that the university will take this as an opportunity to consider that the notion of diversity should, most importantly, include ideology, not just the usual race, gender, and economic categories that my colleagues usually mean by diversity.â

Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco is under fire for allegedly using more than $3 million in taxpayer dollars on campaign expenses, at the same time that he's battling the county over legal fees for his failed ballot investigation. 

A new report from the Riverside County Auditor-Controller says Bianco used nearly $3.2 million to cover trips for himself and his security detail over the 12-month period he was running for governor. Expenses were used to cover gubernatorial debates, podcast appearances and other political events unrelated to county business, according to a report requested by County Supervisor Jose Medina. 

Undersheriff Don Sharp, a spokesperson for Bianco, defended the expenditures in a statement shared with CBS LA. 

"Sheriff Bianco has received death threats dating back to his opposition to COVID mandates and his efforts to stand up for Riverside County residents," the statement said, in part. "Those threats have continued and intensified over time, resulting in arrests both in California and out of state. ... Serving as the elected Sheriff is not a job that ends at the close of business. Sheriff Bianco holds that responsibility 24 hours a day, 365 days a year."

For every incident of homophobia that gets spoken about, there are countless others that go unreported, unchallenged or are quietly dismissed. Every day, people across this country and around the world are made to feel uncomfortable, unwelcome or unsafe simply because of who they are or who they love and so often, theyâre expected to tolerate it, laugh it off or accept an apology and move on.

Discrimination doesnât always announce itself. Sometimes it exists in the language people use behind closed doors, in the attitudes we choose to overlook, and in the failure to take people seriously when they speak up.

Progress is something we should be proud of, but it should never make us complacent. Equality is about more than the rights weâre given. Itâs about the dignity, respect and safety weâre afforded in everyday life.

Weâre sharing this because these experiences deserve to be taken seriously, whoever they happen to. Weâre sharing this because nobody should have to fight to be treated with the basic respect every human being deserves.

Thereâs still so much work to be done, sadly.

From the Interfraternity Councils at ASU, NAU of UA:

On behalf of thousands of fraternity men and future students at Arizona State University, Northern Arizona University and the University of Arizona, we reject the announced decision to restrict fraternity recruitment.

Research shows deferred recruitment does not improve student safety or outcomes. Fraternities improve retention and help first-year students make the transition to college, which is why dozens of campuses are ending deferred recruitment. Students should decide for themselves when to join, just as they can with any other student activity.

We call on Arizonaâs university leaders to reverse this decision and to start a real dialogue with students, alumni and other stakeholders. A decision this significant should be made in partnership, and this one was not. That calls into question whether we can remain long-term partners.

This Wednesday, San Francisco broke a 108-year-old rainfall record for Nov. 18. According to the National Weather Service, Downtown San Francisco received 2.64 inches of rain in one day, topping the 2.24-inch record set in 1918. 

Flooding affected areas throughout the city, impacting the lives of students and teachers at Lowell. On Wednesday morning, the home of Ethnic Studies and AP Psychology teacher Carolina Samayoa flooded with rainwater and sewage. âIt was up to my partnerâs kneeâ¦ and it completely destroyed all of our furniture. My pets were in there, so it was pretty scary,â she said. Samayoa has been displaced from her home until early December while repairs are made.

At Lowell, AP Environmental Science (APES) classroom 260 had an inch of standing water. âWe get seepage underneath the threshold; it comes into the classroom, and it finds its way underneath some of our cabinetry,â said APES teacher Lindsay Sandzik. She put out sandbags to keep the water out. âBut the water has damaged the floor,â she said.

According to ABC7 News, the heavy rains were partly influenced by El NiÃ±o, a repeated climate pattern that happens roughly every seven years, influencing weather conditions in certain regions of the country. âWe should expect warmer, wetter weather, in particular in Southern California, but weâre certainly witnessing that wet weather here right now,â said Sandzik. The National Weather Service says 1 to 3 inches could fall in parts of the Bay Area Nov. 24â25. This rainfall could be accompanied by exceptionally high tides, often called king tides. 

Caption and photos by Faye Yang

Over the past year, UC Berkeley has struggled to navigate the changing role of AI within academics, confronting failing grades that some professors have attributed to studentsâ reliance on AI and a math professor refusing to grade homework because of the prevalence of AI cheating, among other battles.

On the latest frontier of AI at Berkeley, campus has announced a new AI-grading tool that will be piloted this spring semester with up to 15 faculty members at the Haas School of Business.

The tool, called Rubrica, is intended to decrease grading time for GSIs by 40-60% as written exams become increasingly common among professors attempting to fight back against the rise of AI.

Rubrica is a desktop app that compares studentsâ work against professorsâ own rubrics to grade written exams and provide feedback. According to Tom Tripp, executive director of Haas Digital, class materials that the AI works with will be entirely anonymous, and studentsâ identifying information will be held locally on professorsâ computers.

Course instructors must review Rubricaâs work before its grades are released.

Tripp added that the tool contains safeguards, including flagging poor handwriting and allowing professors to review any unclear results. Rubrica can also provide large-scale statistics and diagnostic reports to professors.

On behalf of thousands of fraternity men, and current and future students, at Arizona State University, Northern Arizona University and the University of Arizona, we reject the announced decision to restrict fraternity recruitment.

Research shows that deferred and delayed recruitment does not improve safety or other student outcomes. Students should decide for themselves whether and when fraternity membership is right for them, and the sooner they have that choice, the better. Fraternities improve student retention and help first-year students make the transition to college. That is why dozens of campuses have been ending deferred recruitment. Access to fraternities should be no different from access to any other student activity.

In a historic shift that has sent shockwaves across the Pacific-12 alumni network, Arizona State University has officially dethroned USC as UCLAâs fiercest, most cutthroat academic rival.

The escalation began when ASUâs administration realized their aggressive expansion into downtown Los Angeles meant Sun Devils were physically encroaching on West Coast turf. Seeking total institutional dominance, ASU dispatched a strike force of three hundred hyper-optimized online-degree coordinators to Westwood, launching a blitzkrieg of targeted ads that temporarily paralyzed UCLAâs enrollment portal.

The rivalry turned hostile during the annual West Coast Academic Summit, where UCLA department chairs attempted to flex their traditional research rankings, only for ASU representatives to unveil a multi-million-dollar holographic billboard declaring Tempe the #1 university in the country for âInnovation and Solar-Powered Hustleâ for the tenth consecutive year.

Refusing to back down, UCLAâs economics department attempted a counter-offensive by deploying high-frequency analytical models to discredit ASUâs degree outputs. However, the Sun Devils neutralized the attack in minutes by flooding the Westwood quad with thousands of customized electric scooters programmed to play the ASU fight song at top volume whenever a Bruin tried to study for finals.

Now, instead of prepping for the traditional Crosstown Showdown against USC, UCLA students are spending their weekends building defense perimeters around Powell Library to keep out rogue ASU recruiters offering free hydro-flasks and instant double-majors in Innovation Management to anyone passing by.

label_values.value: Job interviews are basically two strangers pretending this is a completely normal conversation while silently judging each other. You spend hours preparing answers to questions like âTell me about yourselfâ and âWhere do you see yourself in five years?â, only to be asked something completely unexpected like âIf you were an animal, what would you be?â You rehearse your answers in the mirror, research the company, prepare questions to ask and convince yourself youâre going to absolutely nail it. Then the interviewer joins the call and suddenly you forget your own name, your qualifications and every single thing youâve ever accomplished. Somehow, you manage to explain your entire personality in 30 seconds, smile awkwardly and end the interview with âThank you for your time.â Then comes the worst part: waiting for an email that may or may not arrive, checking your inbox every 10 minutes and overanalysing every answer you gave. And after all that, the company sends you a rejection email saying theyâve decided to move forward with another candidate. At this point, getting rejected feels like part of the interview process.

Muay Thai, which translates to âThai Boxingâ, is the national sport of Thailand. It is a martial art with roots originating from wartime of the 13th century during the time of the Sukhothai Kingdom. In modern times, it has been adapted to a competitive sport, but the technique still applies in self defense situations through standup striking.

Muay Thai is known as the âArt of 8 limbsâ because it makes use of 8 points of contact. Punches, elbows, knees and kicks. Clinching, sweeps and throws are also used in modern Muay Thai, making it a fully rounded martial art.

Muay Thai is a great way to learn how to defend yourself while offering lots of health benefits as well! It builds physical fitness and cardiovascular endurance through full body conditioning, while also providing an outlet for self expression, helping increase confidence and mental clarity.

Spirit shut down in May, ending about 17,000 jobs. In August, Google won a bankruptcy auction for its internal data, listed in court filings as about 100 million emails and 500 million Microsoft Teams chat and collaboration records.

Passenger data was excluded, and Google said personal information would be scrubbed first. A flight attendantsâ union objected over worker privacy, and more than 100 lawmakers urged a halt, warning that removing names does not necessarily make data anonymous.

The deal included employee records. After union and lawmaker pushback, Google agreed to exclude medical and disability history, drug tests and payroll, the union said. A judge approved the sale Nov. 17; Google hasnât said which products will use it.

AI companies are increasingly paying for peopleâs data to train their systems, and even the emails and messages left behind by a failed company are now an asset that can be sold.

Grand Theft Auto VI builds its world out of systems that keep running whether Jason and Lucia are watching or not.

Police in Leonida act only on what they actually saw, and a search winds down once you leave the area. NPCs post to their own in-game social media feed, get arrested by police themselves, and confront Jason after a crash. Random encounters stop traffic: protesters block a highway to free a bear from an animal services truck, and Jason can talk to both sides or open the truck doors himself.

Mana Sakura was studying civil engineering at a technical college when she made her debut in February 2012, aged eighteen. The secret lasted barely a week. Classmates recognised her, teachers heard the rumours, and whether the student on screen was really her was even discussed at a staff meeting. Confronted directly, she smiled and denied it â and kept denying it until she graduated.

Instead of retreating, she later told the story herself. Her 2015 autobiographical essay described the discovery at school and why she came to see the work as her calling. In 2016 her first novel, The Lowlife, drew critical praise and was adapted into a film the following year. Sakura has since published several more novels and built a mainstream second career as a television commentator and news anchor.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) proposed pushing back by five years the legal deadline to close Rikers Island, the cityâs infamous and long-troubled jail complex, and outlined his plan to replace the facility with smaller jails based in each borough.

Mamdaniâs proposal moves the deadline from 2027 to 2032 to allow time to build the borough-based jails, starting with a facility in Brooklyn slated to open in 2029. The plan calls for reducing the jail population from more than 6,000 to about 4,100.

New York City officials argue that creating smaller jails will make it easier for incarcerated people to maintain family relationships and access support and legal services, leading to better outcomes once they are released.

Officials also plan to more than triple the number of outpatient therapeutic housing units across the city, where prisoners with serious mental health issues can be transferred.

Unhinged things I did to get a 120 on my Orgo 2 exam (curved + bonus points)ð§ª

For premeds who are willing to go to extremes to get the grade. I donât recommend this. I only did this because there was a period of time where I was working full time night shifts and also trying to study for the MCAT on top of classes.

What I actually did:
1ï¸â£ Created an alter ego: a separate identity with no emotion attached. When itâs time to work, it takes over and uses my body like a vessel. No negotiation on whether I feel like working.
2ï¸â£ Studied in the same library every day, floor and seats included. When it felt like prison, I started studying outside to keep myself sane.
3ï¸â£ for these past 2 years I said no to football games, college events and hanging out. All I do is study, volunteer, go to the gym, and make time for family 
4ï¸â£ Spent morning to night in the library, napping on the library couch when Iâd been operating in a fog.
5ï¸â£ Reminded myself of a documentary I watched about factory workers who work 16 hours a day, 7 days a week, for 30 days straight before getting a day off.
6ï¸â£ Made working out as painful as possible to get my mind off school. It shut my brain off.

About 90% of my weeks were six days of studying, by myself, even while working full time nights. This semester Iâm also studying for the MCAT on top of these classes, while volunteering. Itâs taken a toll on me mentally.

Adcoms reward outcomes, theyâre not going to ask whether you were âtiredâ. You either win or lose.

SANTA CRUZ, CA â The Santa Cruz City Council has advanced plans for a permanent Santa Cruz Warriors arena and massive downtown entertainment district, bringing the city one step closer to becoming San Jose with an ocean view. The arena would replace a facility that's somehow remained temporary since 2012, while the surrounding redevelopment could add up to 1,200 housing units, restaurants, and commercial spaces. Apparently, Santa Cruz's transformation into Santana Row with better surfing is right on schedule.

Supporters point to projections of more than $43 million in annual economic activity and hundreds of jobs. Impressive numbers, although they don't explain whether the average Santa Cruz worker will be able to afford living anywhere near all this prosperity. Then there's "affordable housing," a term that has become something of a linguistic mystery along the California coast, where an apartment apparently qualifies as reasonably priced so long as the tenant earns enough to purchase a small yacht.

Meanwhile, questions remain about traffic, aging infrastructure, and whether Santa Cruz can preserve the independent businesses and local character that made it desirable in the first place. Fortunately, future residents will have plenty of upscale restaurants where they can discuss how much they love the city's authentic beach-town charm.

Construction hasn't been approved, financing remains unresolved, and the final price tag is anyone's guess. But Santa Cruz is one step closer to enjoying all the amenities of Silicon Valley without having to drive over Highway 17.

They'll just have to figure out how to afford living there.

the way people treat successful women in the industry as opposed to men is insane

Zendaya has recently faced criticism over how frequently she appears in major Hollywood productions, with some social media users accusing the actress of being overexposed. The discussion has intensified amid speculation about her potentially becoming the next Bond girl, with critics questioning why Hollywood continues to cast the same familiar faces. However, others have pointed out an interesting double standard when comparing the reactions to Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, who has also secured numerous major roles in recent years. While Pattinson is often praised for his versatility, impressive career choices, and ability to stay booked, Zendaya frequently faces accusations of being overrated or appearing in too many projects. Some fans believe this reflects a broader pattern in Hollywood where successful actresses, particularly women of color, face harsher scrutiny for achieving the same level of success as their male counterparts. The debate has raised questions about whether audiences are genuinely experiencing celebrity fatigue or simply holding certain performers to different standards.

KINGMAN, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) â A school janitor in northwestern Arizona is accused of giving vape pens and alcohol to girls in exchange for naked photos of them.

The Mohave County Sheriffâs Office said Thursday that Pierce Anthony Eller, 41, is facing more than a dozen charges.

Investigators said Eller works as a janitor at a Kingman-area school through a private contractor, and the vape-for-explicit-photos trades started in February with an underage family friend.

The sheriffâs office said there have been 10 trades between Eller and the victim.

Detectives said the victim then told her friends about the deal, and the friends reached out to Eller on social media.

The sheriffâs office said Eller gave three additional girls, ages 14 to 16, vapes and alcohol in exchange for nude photos of them.

Deputies said Eller admitted to the allegations Wednesday and that they found more evidence on his phone.

He was arrested and booked into jail on 10 counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, four counts of luring a minor and four counts of commercial exploitation of a minor.

Deputies said none of the victims were students at the school where Eller worked.

This summer, four teenagers set up two folding chairs on a BART station concourse and started asking strangers to sit down. The result was âBART and Soul,â an eight-minute documentary about the people who ride BART and the places it takes them.Â Â 
Â 
âBART and Soulâ was created by a four-person crew of teen filmmakers: Juno Leto Finney, Lalita Haar, Xia Snyder, and Katie Vong. The film emerged from @campreelstories, a @bavcmedia program that gives girls and gender nonconforming youth hands-on filmmaking experience over two weeks each summer. In that time, the crew, wrote, shot, and cut the whole thing, trading roles as they went. They released it under the name Dead Seagulls Studios. It doesnât mean anything (but it made them laugh).
Â 
âBARTâs not just transportation,â Lalita said of their decision to center BART in the documentary. âItâs a whole community of people that have something in common and can learn something from each other.â
Â 
Thatâs the thread running throughout the film; on a BART train youâre surrounded by strangers, all of whom have a destination in mind and a story to tell.Â Â 
Â 
It wasnât hard to unearth those stories. The filmmakers set up shop and then approached passersby with a sign that read, âTell us your coolest BART story?â
Â 
âWhen you sit on BART and look around, at first it could look like youâre surrounded by strangers,â the voiceover at the end says. âHowever, the beautiful thing our documentary helped us highlight is weâre all connected by the relationships and memories weâve gained from this transportation system. BART is connection.âÂ 
Â 
Watch the full documentary at the link in bio

Opinion 
ASUCD campaigns are all slop and no substance

Being an informed voter is difficult when campaigns donât stand for anything
BY NEVEN BISINOVSKI
GRAPHIC: Olivia Barnett

The recent Associated Students of UC Davis (ASUCD) Senate campaigns were an embarrassment to student democracy.

Scrolling through slatesâ Instagram pages, like those of AVANZA, EMPOWERED, STFU (Stop Taking From Us) or GOAT (Greater Opportunities, Affordability and Transparency) yields little information from which voters can form a decision regarding their candidates of choice.

A vast majority of candidates ran on the same agreeable and vague promises to bring down costs, increase opportunities and cultivate a more equitable environment for students. However, campaign materials lacked both detailed explanations regarding these promises and tangible plans for their fruition.

Never in a million years did I imagine Iâd be working on a project with Yale that has the potential to transform how local communities get access to public health information. Weâre bringing together emerging tech, data modeling, public health and local journalism through a project with the esteemed Yale School of Public Health and Pulitzer-winning Connecticut Mirror newsroom. Itâs the kind of work Iâve been dreaming of doing. I come from humble beginnings as a daughter of Indian immigrants, and went through public schools and a great public state university. When I stepped foot on Yaleâs campus a few weeks ago to lead the kickoff of our project, the word âprivilegeâ followed me around everywhere I went. Somewhere between getting lost in the stunning libraries, our kickoff meeting, and gallivanting around what felt like Hogwarts, I started rethinking what access to education really means in this era of technological disruption and chaos. We keep calling AI this great âequalizerâ but weâre confusing access to information as access to education. Thatâs what Iâm diving into for this weekâs essay. Join me. Full essay linked in my bio. 

>> A very special shoutout to @megranney for opening this door for me and being such an incredible mentor + my team at @weareajp for giving me the autonomy and resources to follow my curiosity into work like this. Having people trust you enough to explore a possibility and give you room to pursue it is an extraordinary privilege

A 10-year-old Star Wars fan refused to fight back after being attacked by a bully at school because he believed violence wasn't the Jedi way.

In 2018, Aiden Vazquez, a fifth-grade student from California, was hospitalized after another student punched him in the face, leaving him with injuries that required stitches.

When his mother asked why he hadn't defended himself, Aiden explained that he had learned from Star Wars that fighting back wasn't the Jedi way.

His story quickly spread online and eventually reached Mark Hamill, the actor behind Luke Skywalker.

Hamill praised Aiden for his courage and wisdom, calling him a real-life Jedi and celebrating his decision not to respond to violence with more violence.

The moment became a reminder of how fictional heroes can inspire real-life acts of courage and kindness.

The University of Oregonâs graduate employees union has declared an intent to strike if it doesnât reach a deal on a new contract by Nov. 16.

The Graduate Teaching Fellows Federation represents around 1,200 student employees. This includes research assistants, graders, and instructors teaching some classes, labs and discussion sections.

The union is currently negotiating with UO for a new contract. But Amelia Cuomo, a co-chair for GTFFâs bargaining team, said theyâve been unable to reach agreement on some core financial issues.

98% of participating union members voted this week in favor of a strike, according to a union press release early Saturday morning.

Cuomo said if workers hit the picket line this month, it could slow down grading or force the university to cancel classes in the middle of Fall Term.

âComing towards the end of the term is grading crunch time,â Cuomo said. âStudents want their final grades. They have midterms and final exams that theyâre taking. And if we go on strike then, withholding all of that information is a more powerful strike.â

The university and unionâs disagreements center on healthcare, job security, and salaries.

UO is asking employees to pay for a larger percentage of their health insurance. It says the unionâs latest insurance plan has increased the schoolâs annual costs by $1.6 million.

Meanwhile, the union is asking the university to form a workgroup to lower healthcare spending in the future. But in the meantime, it wants UO to take on a larger share for the rest of this fiscal year.

The university and the union are in agreement about offering no raise this fiscal year. But the university is offering two 2.5% raises in the two following years, while the union is asking for 3.5% and 4% increases.

The unionâs announcement comes after UOâs classified employees union barely averted a strike earlier this year. The faculty union also reached a last-minute deal to avert a strike last year, while student workers hit the picket lines for more than a week.
